title: Mentoring the Machine — Eric Hou, Augment Code

summary: Eric Hou, a member of technical staff at Augment Code, presents a framework for integrating AI agents into software engineering at scale. He opens with his background building large-scale automotive systems and frames the talk in four sections: personal journey, agent usage practices, organizational gaps, and addressing those gaps. He anchors the talk in a relatable Tuesday scenario—a delayed design system component, a staging emergency, and a new hire needing help—all hitting simultaneously. After describing the painful version with 23-minute recovery costs per interruption and $300 billion annually spent on maintenance, he replays the same day using Augment agents: scoping the design component into an RFC, parallelizing log parsing and git bisect, directing the new hire to a context-engine-backed Slackbot, and completing a gRPC remediation across 12 services and 20,000 lines in roughly half a day. The engineer's role shifts from implementation to evaluation and orchestration. The core realization is that AI should be treated like junior engineers—mentored with outcomes, context, and constraints. Both AI and new hires lack organizational context, but AI processes instantly yet forgets between conversations, making it a perpetually junior engineer; engineers must become perpetual tech leads. Individual gains stall at team scale because the context/knowledge gap remains unsolved. He then details a three-step adoption pattern: (1) knowledge gathering—mapping existing knowledge sources, capturing meetings with intelligence tools, and integrating data sources via MCP and native integrations; (2) gaining familiarity—introducing tools across teams, teaching coding patterns and architectural decisions, and building the muscle of working with AI; (3) leaning in—expanding successful patterns, entrusting complex tasks, and sharing memories and task lists across teams for compound learning. A live demo creates a new agent personality from a simple prompt, illustrating how implementation can happen during a talk. He closes by arguing that once knowledge infrastructure is solved, information transfer becomes instant and scalable, enabling parallel exploration—rapidly prototyping, testing, and converging on decisions based on real metrics rather than room arguments. This turns retrospective wishes about design decisions into proactive, data-informed choices, making software creation more of a science, not less.

sections.title: Introduction and background
sections.summary: Eric introduces himself as a member of technical staff at Augment Code, which builds for real software engineering at scale. He references his prior six years building automotive systems touched by tens of thousands of engineers where no one understands more than 5% of the system, framing his understanding of hands-on engineering work.

sections.title: Talk structure and the painful Tuesday scenario
sections.summary: Eric outlines four sections: personal journey, agent usage practices, organizational gaps, and addressing those gaps. He then describes a chaotic Tuesday—a delayed design system component, a staging emergency from a client/server request format mismatch, and a new hire needing help—illustrating industry-wide context-switching costs of 23 minutes per interruption and $300 billion annually.

sections.title: Tuesday replayed with AI agents
sections.summary: Eric replays the same Tuesday using Augment agents: scoping the design component into an RFC, parallelizing log parsing and git bisect, routing the new hire to a context-engine-backed Slackbot, and completing a gRPC library remediation across 12 services and 20,000 lines in roughly half a day. His role shifts from implementation to evaluation and orchestration.

sections.title: Core realization: mentoring the machine
sections.summary: Eric distills the approach: work with AI as with junior engineers—mentoring, not assigning tickets. Both lack organizational context and need structured environments, but AI processes instantly yet forgets between conversations, making it a perpetually junior engineer. Engineers must become perpetual tech leads and mentors.

sections.title: Organizational scaling and knowledge infrastructure
sections.summary: Eric identifies the context/knowledge gap as the same blocker causing six-month new-hire ramp-up and cited by four out of five engineers as the biggest blocker. Scaling AI beyond individuals requires institutionalizing knowledge infrastructure via the right tools, not more docs or reorgs. He previews a three-step pattern for companies to get started.

sections.title: Three-step adoption pattern
sections.summary: Eric details the three steps: (1) knowledge gathering—mapping existing knowledge sources, filling gaps with meeting intelligence tools, and integrating data via MCP and native integrations; (2) gaining familiarity—introducing tools across teams, teaching the platform coding patterns and architectural decisions, and building the muscle of working with AI; (3) leaning in—expanding successful patterns, entrusting complex tasks, and sharing memories and task lists across teams for compound learning.

sections.title: Live demo and the economics of parallel exploration
sections.summary: Eric demos creating an agent personality from a simple prompt during the talk, then argues that solving knowledge infrastructure unlocks AI's true economic potential. Parallel exploration replaces the traditional design-build-test sequence with rapid prototyping, testing, and convergence on real metrics. He cites Augment prototypes like a VS Code fork and agents itself, and closes by arguing effective AI use makes software creation more of a science, not less. He invites attendees to visit the Augment booth and notes remote agents launched this week.
